Murder Rate Justice 14.5%

By: Carol Albertyn Christie | Paid

Proposal


Show:

Summary:
Ian Cameron

Ian Cameron is the founder of Action Society. Started in 2019, the NPO says that they “work within the community to fight for a reformed justice system.”

The latest International Security Studies report indicates that only 14.5% of murders are brought to justice.

https://www.saps.gov.za/services/downloads/Annual-Crime-2021_2022-web.pdf

https://issafrica.org/iss-today/soaring-murder-rates-underline-the-lack-of-sound-direction-for-policing#:~:text=There%20has%20also%20been%20a,56%20deaths%20per%20100%20000.

“That's shocking. That means that today, according to the latest crime stats, we've got 84 murders a day in South Africa. That's three and a half murders per hour.
So let's round it off to four murders per hour in the country. That means out of that four murders, not even one of them will likely be solved. That’s how horrific it is. So you and I can literally walk out. We can shoot and kill someone. And if I don't hand myself over to the police, chances are that I'll walk free and not.”

Ian acknowledges that the police are overworked and there are backlogs but his experience is that there is a lack of empathy with the police.

“But what hit me was it felt like there was no compassion for the state for what was happening to people. But from an Action Society point of view, this is the trend that's increasing throughout the country that victims are just they are just that they are just it's just another victim. We're just another murder. It's kind of normal. And we can never, ever, ever allow that to become the norm.”

In some cases Action Society has offered to assist the police in their investigations and the offer has just been blown off. Ian believes that one can only attribute it to 3 things either incompetence, a lack of interest or corruption.

Ian on Police leadership

“And then I must ask what and I'm going to say this very bluntly the leadership is is absolutely useless, useless. There's no doubt. And according to my experience and from my point of view, any good leader, regardless of how what a senior rank though anyone that oversees this matter would see. But there is something very wrong, and we need to intervene.

But they don't even have the integrity to do such a basic thing. So how do we expect change on the ground level with regard to policing and crime if they can't even do something?”

Prosecution

“And I often get the excuse from the police that, yeah, but it's the prosecutor. But then when we speak with a prosecutor and we look, we we we inquire about the dockets, the prosecutor says, I can't prosecute someone if I don't have a docket that makes any sense.

There's nothing written in there. There's zero logic in their dockets. I mean, all of our police, especially new recruits, don't even have the skill to write properly. How on earth are they going to testify in court or oppose bail? Now, where do the families of murder victims turn if they can no longer trust the police to do a proper investigation?”

Action Society admits that they have too many cases. Those that they do take on they attend every single court appearance and stay with them to the end.

Ian has a board in his office with 8 or 9 cases that keep him up at night.

Ian
So for me personally, I believe God gave me an opportunity to make an impact so that God motivates me. And I stand firm with that.

If we've got a community, we need to be guardians and custodians of that community. We need to protect people. I know there's intimidation. We face it every single day. But I don't I don't buy the fact that that outweighs the calling that we have to bring justice.

Reverend Liezel de Jager’s murder as an illustration of the Police’s ineptitude.

Ian Cameron of Action SA brought this story to CB’s attention.

Cameron's perspective sheds light on a troubling pattern, suggesting that Liezel's tragic fate was treated with a concerning lack of empathy and compassion by Police authorities.

Understanding that the Police is under-resourced and have a large workload, Action Society SA went above and beyond to support the investigation. They offered to assist the police by compiling a comprehensive case file, assisting in transport, and basically compiling a docket for the police. These offers were ignored by the police.

In Cameron's assessment, the root causes of this poor performance lies either in incompetence, disinterest, and potential corruption within the law enforcement system. He highlights a disheartening reality where criminal acts can potentially go unpunished if the victim lacks political connections. This raises significant concerns about the accessibility of justice for ordinary citizens.

The de Jager case emulates a larger trend observed in South Africa, where victims seem to be sidelined and overlooked. This distressing pattern indicates a pressing need for reform and a renewed commitment to ensuring justice for those who have suffered.




Liezel’s story

In October 2021, a tragic incident unfolded that shook the community. Reverend Liezel de Jager lost her life outside her house, and the perpetrator behind this heinous act remains unidentified to this day.

The events of that fateful day, the 13th of October 2021, provide a chilling sequence of occurrences:

At around 4:00 in the morning, Liezel embarked on her regular jogging routine. She returned home around 5:45, presumably completing her exercise.

Not long after that, before 6:00, a panic button was pressed, prompting a call from 39 Dan Pienaar to report an accidental activation. Liezel’s husband told the security company that it was an accidental activation. Concurrently, neighbours recalled hearing what might have been a scream, though it was suggested that local monkeys could be responsible for the noise. Although nearby dogs barked in response, notably absent were the sounds from Liezel de Jager's dogs. The neighbours commented that this was strange because when their dogs barked the de Jager’s dogs usually joined in.

Approximately an hour later, at around 7:00, Werner, Liezel's husband, discovered her lifeless body on the floor. Tragically, Liezel had fallen victim to strangulation, a toy spade found near her, indicating its involvement in the crime. The positioning of her bag and keys implied that she was likely strangled upon arriving home. Intriguingly, robbery seemed an unlikely motive, as nothing appeared to have been stolen.

Suspicion surrounding Werner deepened due to certain physical evidence. He displayed abrasions on his knuckles and scratch marks on his right elbow.

There are two panic buttons at home. One is inside the home and the other on Liezel’s key ring. The security company cannot differentiate where the signal came from.

Werner says he slept late and did not hear any noises. He readied their two daughters for school and then he went out and found his wife’s body on the ground.

Then, on the 26th of October, as Werner was scheduled for a polygraph examination, he suddenly vanished on the 24th of October.

Eventually, on the 28th of October, Werner was discovered in sugarfields, bearing injuries including a head bump, broken ribs, and a collarbone fracture. He said he had been attacked and kidnapped by the same individuals responsible for Liezel's death. Then pressured to drink a solution of medication and water.

Werner's narrative implicated a drug known as psyquet, and he in the past has disclosed struggles with schizophrenia and bipolar disorder. Consequently, Liezel's parents were granted custody of their children. Statistically, cases of strangulation and femicide often involve intimate partners, positioning the odds against Werner. His history of mental health challenges further raised suspicions.

In previous years, Werner had made multiple suicide attempts. Notably, in 2015, he bore cut marks on his arms, attributing them to a traumatic incident involving alleged rape and an attack by a group of men. In response, he reported the incident to the police, who, after extensive investigation, faced charges for their perceived inaction. Werner later retracted these charges, revealing a lack of truth in his initial claims. He admitted to making it up and asked forgiveness from his church in the Orange River. A subsequent suicide attempt occurred in 2018, involving a gas bottle in his car.

After relocating to Amanzimtoti for a fresh start, Liezel reportedly expressed intentions of divorce. Werner was absent from work frequently and this was placing financial pressure on Liezel.

On the day of the murder, a peculiar incident unfolded when an alarm went off; security professionals deemed it a silent alarm, though Werner claimed it had awakened him.

Two panic buttons existed – one within the house and another on Liezel's keyring. It remains uncertain which button was pressed during the attack.

Werner's account of his post-Liezel death kidnapping was met with scepticism. His assertion of being attacked, forcibly administered medication, and kidnapped seemed perplexing. Questions arose as to why his assailants wouldn't have simply chosen a more direct method, like the way they strangled his wife.

It is speculated that Werner's injuries might have been self-inflicted, potentially linked to a suicide attempt involving a fall from a significant height. This conjecture aimed to explain the nature of his injuries.

Complicating matters, Liezel's father, a former policeman, voiced concerns over the police's handling of the case. Henk, Liezel's father, made numerous calls to law enforcement, a total of 91, and even reached out to the district commissioner. Disappointingly, the police's response seemed lacking, with a court-ordered cell phone analysis dragging on for an unexpectedly extended period. Over the past half-year, the bereaved family received no updates on the investigation into Liezel's tragic demise.

Although the police has said they were finished with the autopsy, they took the body back from the funeral home to conduct more tests on it. Despite the passage of 17 months, a comprehensive autopsy report remained elusive.

Henk decried the disheartening state of affairs, expressing a dwindling faith in the police institution. His decades of experience afforded him insights into the inner workings of the police system, leading him to believe that justice eludes the average citizen. Henk does not want special treatment, but merely the rights to which every South African is entitled.

While still uninvestigated, Werner caused a car accident in April this year in which Caitlin Eales and her mother-in-law died.
The accident report shows that Werner was driving at 140 km/h and clipped the back of the Eales’ Fortuner.
At the accident Werner did not get out of the car to help and gave incorrect information to the deceased husband on where to find him.

Guy Eales only found out about Werner’s past when he did an internet search on him.

Had the Police conducted a proper investigation, these deaths may have been avoided.

Henk van Zyl – Liezel’s father

Rina, who drove behind Liezel’s car to make sure she arrived home safely after run.

Press Release:


In October 2021, a frantic call from a distraught husband sent emergency services and police to pastor Liezel de Jager’s house. But it was already too late. Liezel was found strangled outside her Amanzimtoti home. Her father Henk van Zyl, a former detective, made over 90 calls to police for feedback, but for two years, the investigation stalled… until civil rights organisation Action Society got involved. With increased pressure and media attention, police finally arrested a suspect last week. It’s an all-too-familiar picture: a case that clearly illustrates the fallout from an overburdened detective service unable to keep up with South Africa’s ever-soaring crime rates. According to the police’s own latest statistics, just under 12.5 percent of the country’s murders are solved. As families mourning the brutal deaths of their loved ones wait months or even years for closure, does the answer lie in watchdog organisations that effectively privatise the investigation and prosecution of crime? Carte Blanche investigates.

Script:


VOICEOVER: In just the last three years, Carte Blanche has covered dozens of stories of murder.
UPSOUND: HENK VAN ZYL: This is not a unique case. It's supposed to be a relatively simple murder case.
VOICEOVER: It’s a drop in the ocean: around 75 people are murdered every day in South Africa.
UPSOUND: GUY EALES: It's not the way that the world should work in my mind.
VOICEOVER: And according to the police’s own latest statistics, just under 12.5% of those murders are solved.
UPSOUND: IAN CAMERON: If you want to kill someone, do it in South Africa because you’re likely to get away with it.
FADE TO BLACK
VOICEOVER: Two years ago, Liezel de Jager was strangled outside her home in Amanzimtoti, where she lived with her husband Werner and their children. The day of her murder, the house alarm was triggered around the same time Liezel got home from her early morning jog.
LINK: This call room received a panic activation from the De Jager home at 6:07AM. When security called there was no answer from either Werner or Liezel. But two minutes later, at 6:09AM, Werner called to say the panic button had been pressed by mistake.
VOICEOVER: Fifteen minutes after that, Werner called again…
UPSOUND: EMERGENCY CALLS: Werner: I need help please, my wife’s been attacked in our garden!
Security centre: What’s happening there, sir?
Werner: She’s dead! It looks like she’s dead.
LINK: Liezel’s body was found by her husband just by that small wall over here. Robbery wasn’t a motive as her car keys and her bag were still lying next to her.
VOICEOVER: Suspicion fell on Werner, whose struggles with mental health had caused tension in the marriage. When police asked him to undergo a polygraph, he disappeared. Days later he was found living in his car in a sugar cane field, claiming that Liezel’s killers had tried to harm him. Police didn’t confirm whether he has since undergone the polygraph, but said a “key suspect” was interviewed in October 2021. Then, for two years, the investigation simply stalled.
UPSOUND: HENK VAN ZYL: The most simple investigation processes that need to be in any crime investigation has just not been done.
VOICEOVER: Liezel’s father Henk van Zyl is a retired police officer who’s worked on police reform for the United Nations. We spoke to him in September.
UPSOUND: MASA: So what have they actually done up until this point with this investigation?
UPSOUND: HENK: As far as I know, they handled the crime scene, collected some trace evidence on the crime scene. Take a number of statements. And apparently they sent some electronic devices and some DNA matter to forensics to be analyzed.
VOICEOVER: Henk had made over 90 calls to the police for feedback.
UPSOUND: HENK: The same message that I've received for the last about 12 to 15 months, I'm still receiving: just waiting for the forensics.
UPSOUND: MASA: As a dad, it must make you so angry.
HENK: I mean, I’m totally emotional about this. And I don’t think you can blame me.
UPSOUND: LIZETTE LANCASTER: Victims of crime deserve to expect their crimes to be solved. So it is really important that expectations are met. If they cannot be met by the police, at least they need to be managed.
VOICEOVER: At the Institute for Security Studies, Lizette Lancaster researches emerging crime trends to inform crime prevention policy. The detection rate on all contact crime is under 50%.
UPSOUND: LIZETTE: Detected cases means that the police feel that they have enough evidence included in their case to take it to court. The detection rate is an important indicator for police performance. It provides us not only of what visible policing or boots on the ground the popular term does, but also what goes on with ballistics, forensics and all the other type of competencies.
VOICEOVER: Murder has the worst detection track record.
UPSOUND: LIZETTE: In most cases, it is very hard to detect a murder. You might have suspects, but it doesn't mean that you have evidence. Often when murders occur there are not other witnesses, but of course there are other factors at play, such as ballistics, forensics… So it is far more complex to investigate than other crimes.
VOICEOVER: As civic services crumble around us, South Africans are privatising what we once expected government to provide… even the investigation and prosecution of crime.
UPSOUND: IAN CAMERON: Let’s just make a note because that’s important not to miss.
VOICEOVER: Ian Cameron is director of Community Safety at civil rights organisation Action Society.
UPSOUND: IAN CAMERON: We not only assist police on ground level with the investigation or with any kind of support they need, but we then also do oversight in court and we try and ensure that nothing falls through the cracks.
MASA: So basically a watchdog for the criminal justice system to work.
IAN: Ja. We're not at a point where we can keep everyone accountable. But at least in terms of the police and in parts of courts, we can make a real impact.
VOICEOVER: The frustration of battling an unresponsive system has driven the victims in around 180 cases to Action Society for help - including Henk.
UPSOUND: IAN: We have started a legal process with regards to the South African police service to to force them into getting the job done. We've actually offered to give private forensic help. Now we are at this point where we have to literally tell the whole world just to have a simple murder investigation completed.
VOICEOVER: The increased attention finally had an effect. In an email to Action Society, KwaZulu Natal police apologised for their “lack of professionalism and sympathy” and acknowledged their “tardiness” in investigating the case. In early November, the case was handed over to the Police National Cold Case Task Team and within three weeks, Werner de Jager had been arrested. But not before he had exploded into the life of another family.
UPSOUND: GUY EALES: Why wasn’t he locked up then? If they had done the job then, would my wife still be alive? Would my mom still be alive?
VOICEOVER: In April this year, Guy Eales’s wife Linda and his mother Bernice were killed when a speeding vehicle rear-ended them on the highway, causing their car to veer off the road and roll.
UPSOUND: GUY EALES: I got a call from my daughter, hysterical: Dad, the car’s rolled. Mom’s not moving.
VOICEOVER: Guy’s daughter, mother-in-law, and a friend were seriously injured.
UPSOUND: GUY EALES: It’s hard to describe sort of the intense feelings that come with the realisation that your life partner’s not coming back again.
VOICEOVER: Guy, too, became concerned about the standard of the police investigation.
UPSOUND: GUY: I realized, you know, there was a lot of missing and incorrect information that was actually on their accident report form. And there was nothing in the file, just the two autopsy reports, no witness statements. No warning statements...
VOICEOVER: He commissioned an independent accident report, and asked witnesses to provide sworn statements. Guy quickly learned that the driver who allegedly collided with his wife’s car was none other than Werner de Jager. Googling Werner’s name, he learned the story of Liezel’s unsolved murder. Police told him that they didn’t know where Werner was - so Guy traced him and provided contact details.
UPSOUND: GUY EALES: When I phoned again, they said no he wasn’t there and now he’s avoiding their calls. They think he’s hiding out at George with his mom, so I gave them that number…
MASA: So you’re basically doing police work now, Guy.
GUY: You kind of want some justice and it doesn't look like it’s going to happen on its own.
VOICEOVER: Werner didn’t respond to any of our questions. Seven months after the crash, Free State Police told us their investigation is nearly complete, Werner’s warning statement has been taken, and the case is now with the Director of Public Prosecutions. They said they welcome community cooperation, and commended the investigating officer for handling this investigation quickly.
LINK: We all know the police are under-resourced, under-staffed and having to deal with an overwhelming number of cases.
VOICEOVER: But is the answer to turn away from the police as we have from so many state services?
UPSOUND: LIZETTE: It is not too unreasonable to expect that in a country where almost every government service is outsourced by those that can afford it, that we see private investigations and prosecutions. I would really like to see that effort being ploughed back into the criminal justice system to help strengthen the services that we have.
VOICEOVER: The number of police detectives has dropped by a third since 2016. Those who are left often carry up to 200 dockets at a time. The police are addressing shortages by recruiting and training new and retired detectives.
UPSOUND: LIZETTE: They are talking about better resource management. Better supervision… But it's not going to solve the fact that we do not have people that have the mentoring that they require to investigate complex crimes. And that is why we need permanent capacity. It's going to cost us money, but we need well equipped, well-trained detectives.
VOICEOVER: Werner de Jager has appeared in court, accused of his wife’s murder, and will remain in custody until his next appearance on the 7th of December. Perhaps Liezel’s family will finally get the closure they so desperately need. Meanwhile, these families are still waiting for answers.

His decades of experience afforded him insights into the inner workings of the police system, leading him to believe that justice eludes the average citizen. While still uninvestigated, Werner caused a car accident in April this year in which Caitlin Eales and her mother-in-law died. The accident report shows that Werner was driving at 140 km/h and clipped the back of the Eales’ Fortuner. At the accident Werner did not get out of the car to help and gave incorrect information to the deceased husband on where to find him. But it was already too late. Liezel was found strangled outside her Amanzimtoti home. Her father Henk van Zyl, a former detective, made over 90 calls to police for feedback, but for two years, the investigation stalled… until civil rights organisation Action Society got involved. With increased pressure and media attention, police finally arrested a suspect last week. It’s an all-too-familiar picture: a case that clearly illustrates the fallout from an overburdened detective service unable to keep up with South Africa’s ever-soaring crime rates. According to the police’s own latest statistics, just under 12.5 percent of the country’s murders are solved. As families mourning the brutal deaths of their loved ones wait months or even years for closure, does the answer lie in watchdog organisations that effectively privatise the investigation and prosecution of crime? Carte Blanche investigates. Script: VOICEOVER: In just the last three years, Carte Blanche has covered dozens of stories of murder. UPSOUND: HENK VAN ZYL: This is not a unique case. It's supposed to be a relatively simple murder case. VOICEOVER: It’s a drop in the ocean: around 75 people are murdered every day in South Africa. UPSOUND: GUY EALES: It's not the way that the world should work in my mind. VOICEOVER: And according to the police’s own latest statistics, just under 12.5% of those murders are solved. UPSOUND: IAN CAMERON: If you want to kill someone, do it in South Africa because you’re likely to get away with it. FADE TO BLACK VOICEOVER: Two years ago, Liezel de Jager was strangled outside her home in Amanzimtoti, where she lived with her husband Werner and their children. The day of her murder, the house alarm was triggered around the same time Liezel got home from her early morning jog. LINK: This call room received a panic activation from the De Jager home at 6:07AM. When security called there was no answer from either Werner or Liezel. But two minutes later, at 6:09AM, Werner called to say the panic button had been pressed by mistake. VOICEOVER: Fifteen minutes after that, Werner called again… UPSOUND: EMERGENCY CALLS: Werner: I need help please, my wife’s been attacked in our garden! Security centre: What’s happening there, sir? Werner: She’s dead! It looks like she’s dead. LINK: Liezel’s body was found by her husband just by that small wall over here. Robbery wasn’t a motive as her car keys and her bag were still lying next to her. VOICEOVER: Suspicion fell on Werner, whose struggles with mental health had caused tension in the marriage. When police asked him to undergo a polygraph, he disappeared. Days later he was found living in his car in a sugar cane field, claiming that Liezel’s killers had tried to harm him. Police didn’t confirm whether he has since undergone the polygraph, but said a “key suspect” was interviewed in October 2021. Then, for two years, the investigation simply stalled. UPSOUND: HENK VAN ZYL: The most simple investigation processes that need to be in any crime investigation has just not been done. VOICEOVER: Liezel’s father Henk van Zyl is a retired police officer who’s worked on police reform for the United Nations. We spoke to him in September. UPSOUND: MASA: So what have they actually done up until this point with this investigation? UPSOUND: HENK: As far as I know, they handled the crime scene, collected some trace evidence on the crime scene. Take a number of statements. And apparently they sent some electronic devices and some DNA matter to forensics to be analyzed. VOICEOVER: Henk had made over 90 calls to the police for feedback. UPSOUND: HENK: The same message that I've received for the last about 12 to 15 months, I'm still receiving: just waiting for the forensics. UPSOUND: MASA: As a dad, it must make you so angry. HENK: I mean, I’m totally emotional about this. And I don’t think you can blame me. UPSOUND: LIZETTE LANCASTER: Victims of crime deserve to expect their crimes to be solved. So it is really important that expectations are met. If they cannot be met by the police, at least they need to be managed. VOICEOVER: At the Institute for Security Studies, Lizette Lancaster researches emerging crime trends to inform crime prevention policy. The detection rate on all contact crime is under 50%. UPSOUND: LIZETTE: Detected cases means that the police feel that they have enough evidence included in their case to take it to court. The detection rate is an important indicator for police performance. It provides us not only of what visible policing or boots on the ground the popular term does, but also what goes on with ballistics, forensics and all the other type of competencies. VOICEOVER: Murder has the worst detection track record. UPSOUND: LIZETTE: In most cases, it is very hard to detect a murder. You might have suspects, but it doesn't mean that you have evidence. Often when murders occur there are not other witnesses, but of course there are other factors at play, such as ballistics, forensics… So it is far more complex to investigate than other crimes. VOICEOVER: As civic services crumble around us, South Africans are privatising what we once expected government to provide… even the investigation and prosecution of crime. UPSOUND: IAN CAMERON: Let’s just make a note because that’s important not to miss. VOICEOVER: Ian Cameron is director of Community Safety at civil rights organisation Action Society. UPSOUND: IAN CAMERON: We not only assist police on ground level with the investigation or with any kind of support they need, but we then also do oversight in court and we try and ensure that nothing falls through the cracks. MASA: So basically a watchdog for the criminal justice system to work. IAN: Ja. We're not at a point where we can keep everyone accountable. But at least in terms of the police and in parts of courts, we can make a real impact. VOICEOVER: The frustration of battling an unresponsive system has driven the victims in around 180 cases to Action Society for help - including Henk. UPSOUND: IAN: We have started a legal process with regards to the South African police service to to force them into getting the job done. We've actually offered to give private forensic help. Now we are at this point where we have to literally tell the whole world just to have a simple murder investigation completed. VOICEOVER: The increased attention finally had an effect. In an email to Action Society, KwaZulu Natal police apologised for their “lack of professionalism and sympathy” and acknowledged their “tardiness” in investigating the case. In early November, the case was handed over to the Police National Cold Case Task Team and within three weeks, Werner de Jager had been arrested. But not before he had exploded into the life of another family. UPSOUND: GUY EALES: Why wasn’t he locked up then? If they had done the job then, would my wife still be alive? Would my mom still be alive? VOICEOVER: In April this year, Guy Eales’s wife Linda and his mother Bernice were killed when a speeding vehicle rear-ended them on the highway, causing their car to veer off the road and roll. UPSOUND: GUY EALES: I got a call from my daughter, hysterical: Dad, the car’s rolled. Mom’s not moving. VOICEOVER: Guy’s daughter, mother-in-law, and a friend were seriously injured. UPSOUND: GUY EALES: It’s hard to describe sort of the intense feelings that come with the realisation that your life partner’s not coming back again. VOICEOVER: Guy, too, became concerned about the standard of the police investigation. UPSOUND: GUY: I realized, you know, there was a lot of missing and incorrect information that was actually on their accident report form. And there was nothing in the file, just the two autopsy reports, no witness statements. No warning statements... VOICEOVER: He commissioned an independent accident report, and asked witnesses to provide sworn statements. Guy quickly learned that the driver who allegedly collided with his wife’s car was none other than Werner de Jager. Googling Werner’s name, he learned the story of Liezel’s unsolved murder. Police told him that they didn’t know where Werner was - so Guy traced him and provided contact details. UPSOUND: GUY EALES: When I phoned again, they said no he wasn’t there and now he’s avoiding their calls. They think he’s hiding out at George with his mom, so I gave them that number… MASA: So you’re basically doing police work now, Guy. GUY: You kind of want some justice and it doesn't look like it’s going to happen on its own. VOICEOVER: Werner didn’t respond to any of our questions. Seven months after the crash, Free State Police told us their investigation is nearly complete, Werner’s warning statement has been taken, and the case is now with the Director of Public Prosecutions. They said they welcome community cooperation, and commended the investigating officer for handling this investigation quickly. LINK: We all know the police are under-resourced, under-staffed and having to deal with an overwhelming number of cases. VOICEOVER: But is the answer to turn away from the police as we have from so many state services? UPSOUND: LIZETTE: It is not too unreasonable to expect that in a country where almost every government service is outsourced by those that can afford it, that we see private investigations and prosecutions. I would really like to see that effort being ploughed back into the criminal justice system to help strengthen the services that we have. VOICEOVER: The number of police detectives has dropped by a third since 2016. Those who are left often carry up to 200 dockets at a time. The police are addressing shortages by recruiting and training new and retired detectives. UPSOUND: LIZETTE: They are talking about better resource management. Better supervision… But it's not going to solve the fact that we do not have people that have the mentoring that they require to investigate complex crimes. And that is why we need permanent capacity. It's going to cost us money, but we need well equipped, well-trained detectives. VOICEOVER: Werner de Jager has appeared in court, accused of his wife’s murder, and will remain in custody until his next appearance on the 7th of December. Perhaps Liezel’s family will finally get the closure they so desperately need. Meanwhile, these families are still waiting for answers.

But from an Action Society point of view, this is the trend that's increasing throughout the country that victims are just they are just that they are just it's just another victim. While still uninvestigated, Werner caused a car accident in April this year in which Caitlin Eales and her mother-in-law died. The accident report shows that Werner was driving at 140 km/h and clipped the back of the Eales’ Fortuner. At the accident Werner did not get out of the car to help and gave incorrect information to the deceased husband on where to find him. Guy Eales only found out about Werner’s past when he did an internet search on him. Had the Police conducted a proper investigation, these deaths may have been avoided. Interviews.
